title: Z.ai releases GLM-5.3 open weights after two-week safety hold and 2,436 vulnerability disclosures
subtitle: The Chinese lab published the 743-billion-parameter model on Hugging Face on August 28, alongside a bug ledger covering Linux, WebKit, and FreeBSD that the model itself produced during evaluation.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Z.ai — the Zhipu-descended Chinese lab — pushed the full open weights of GLM-5.3 to Hugging Face on August 28, roughly two weeks later than the API launch on August 14. The model is a 743-billion-parameter Mixture-of-Experts, delivered as an FP8 checkpoint spread across 141 shards totaling about 755 GB. Alongside the release, the lab published a bug ledger documenting 2,436 vulnerabilities the model surfaced across 269 open-source projects during evaluation, with 1,097 rated critical or high severity, and named finds in Linux, WebKit, and FreeBSD.

The mechanism worth reading carefully is what actually held the weights back. Z.ai's post-training run added vulnerability-discovery data expecting a modest bump on CyberGym; instead the model started chaining discovery, validation, and end-to-end exploitation into single multi-stage reasoning traces — capability the lab says it did not explicitly target. CyberGym scores landed at 84.5%, narrowly ahead of Claude Mythos 5 at 83.8% and GPT-5.6 Sol at 83.6%. The two-week hold was used to run a safety assessment before wide release; the lab framed the delay as a promise it had made to regulators and partners.

The context sharpens the story. This is the first frontier-class open-weights release where the developer voluntarily paused a scheduled drop after a capability jump appeared in post-training — and the first where a Chinese lab published a bug ledger alongside the weights rather than the usual model card and benchmarks. It follows the anonymous 'Ox Alpha' stealth-model reveal (which turned out to be an early GLM-5.3-Flash checkpoint), the August 2 enforcement of the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency rules, and a summer of open-vs-closed debate over whether cyber-capable weights should ship without a license restriction. The FreeBSD, WebKit, and Linux disclosures now put upstream maintainers on the clock.

Takeaway for learners: an open-weights release is no longer just a model file — it is now a package that can include a capability ledger, a delayed-release story, and a set of live vulnerabilities that need patching in software you almost certainly run. If you deploy open-source infrastructure, treat the GLM-5.3 disclosures as an actionable feed, not a curiosity. And if you are studying AI safety, the interesting thread is not 'did the lab do the right thing' but the concrete decision procedure: what capability threshold triggered the hold, what evaluation was actually run in those two weeks, and what would have to change for the hold to become a permanent no.
